> AGENT

Typecheck clean.

**Summary of the fix:**

- `useShotSettings.ts:85` passed `inheritedSettings || createDefaultVideoTravelSettings()` as `defaults` to `useAutoSaveSettings`. When `inheritedSettings` was null (most of the time), `createDefaultVideoTravelSettings()` was called on every render → **new object reference every render**.
- That `defaults` reference flows into `useAutoSaveSettings` and is in the deps of `useReactQueryModeLoad`'s effect (`autoSaveSettingsLoaders.ts:173`). New ref every render → effect body re-executes every render → cascades dep churn through `useMemo`'d consumers, ultimately reaching the `VideoTravelSettingsContext` value and the Model Select / textarea.
- Wrapped in `useMemo(() => inheritedSettings || createDefaultVideoTravelSettings(), [inheritedSettings])` — now the reference is stable unless `inheritedSettings` genuinely changes.

**Expected result when you reload**:
- The `[ModeDebug]` logs should fire only a handful of times on initial load, not the 30+ cascade you saw.
- Model Select should stay open when clicked.
- Textarea should accept typing without remount-loss.

Test it and share the log. If the storm is gone → root caused. If it's reduced but still present → there's a second unstable dep somewhere and we keep digging.

Clean. New diagnostic logs added:

- **`[ImageLightbox] render`** — counts renders per lightbox instance. If you see the `instance` value change between clicks, the lightbox is remounting (that's your bug). If `instance` stays the same but `renderCount` climbs fast, it's just re-rendering.
- **`[EditModePanel] render`** — same, for the panel containing the Select.

Reproduce the Select bug and paste:
1. Full log from opening the lightbox.
2. The logs around the Select click.

What I'm looking for:
- **If `instance` changes around the Select click** → the panel is being unmounted (probably by a parent re-render that creates a new element). Bug is "parent recreates the panel tree every Nth render."
- **If `instance` stays the same, renderCount jumps by 10+** on click → severe re-render burst still happening, just from a different source than VideoTravelSettingsProvider.
- **If renderCount jumps by 1–2 only** → not a re-render problem. Then it's something in Base UI Select itself or a DOM-level event interference.

That'll narrow it to the right file to fix.

> AGENT

Found two compounding issues. The `MediaLightbox` in `VideoEditorProvider` passes inline objects/callbacks (`onClose`, `features`) on every render, and `resolvedLightboxMedia = lightboxQuery.data ?? lightboxFallbackMedia` is recomputed inline. Then inside `ImageLightbox`, `useLayoutEffect([media])` calls `setImageDimensions` with a fresh object every time media ref changes → new render → effect fires again.

Fix both:

> TOOL

tool_use Edit
```json
{
  "replace_all": false,
  "file_path": "/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh-workspace/reigh-app/src/domains/media-lightbox/hooks/useImageLightboxEnvironment.ts",
  "old_string": "  useLayoutEffect(() => {\n    const dims = extractDimensionsFromMedia(media, true);\n    if (dims) {\n      setImageDimensions(dims);\n    }\n  }, [media]);",
  "new_string": "  useLayoutEffect(() => {\n    const dims = extractDimensionsFromMedia(media, true);\n    if (!dims) return;\n    setImageDimensions((prev) => {\n      if (prev && prev.width === dims.width && prev.height === dims.height) {\n        return prev;\n      }\n      return dims;\n    });\n  }, [media]);"
}
```

> AGENT

Clean. Three fixes landed:

1. **`useImageLightboxEnvironment.ts`** — `setImageDimensions` now uses a functional updater with value equality check. Even if `extractDimensionsFromMedia` returns a fresh object with the same width/height, state won't change → no re-render → no loop.

2. **`VideoEditorProvider.tsx`** — `onClose` stabilized via `useCallback`, `features` stabilized via `useMemo`. These were fresh references per render, causing MediaLightbox to re-receive "new" props on every parent render.

3. **`initialVariantId`** — extracted to a local const (not memoized, but cheap primitive comparison).

Reload and repeat the test. I'm expecting:
- `[ImageLightbox] render` count to drop from 20 → 3–5 on lightbox open
- `[EditModePanel] render` similar
- Select click: `onOpenChange(true)` stays open until you click an item or click outside

If it works, share the log so we can remove the instrumentation.

> AGENT

Clean. Now each render will log:
- **`[ImageLightbox] render { ..., changedProps: [...] }`** — which props changed vs previous render. Empty `[]` means the parent didn't change props (so something inside caused the render).
- **`[ImageLightbox] env changed { changed: [...] }`** — which env fields changed (e.g. `imageDimensions`, `isDownloading`, `editSettingsPersistence`). This tells us which state transition fired.

Reload and repeat. The patterns to look for:
- If `changedProps: []` repeatedly → the re-render cause is internal to ImageLightbox (an effect setting state).
- If `changed: ['editSettingsPersistence']` repeats → that hook's return is unstable.
- If `changed: ['imageDimensions']` alternates with others → the dimensions state loop is still alive.

Paste the new log output and we'll zero in on the exact offender.

> DEVELOPER

still happening, is there a score structural smell here we're coming up against?

> AGENT

Yes — we keep hitting the same structural smell from different angles.

**The real problem**: the edit-settings pipeline has **five layers of hooks**, each with its own state, each firing its own renders on mount and data changes. Fixing memoization is whack-a-mole because the cascade itself is baked in.

Here's the chain:
```
ImageLightbox
└─ useImageLightboxEnvironment       ← local state + refs + 3 sub-hooks
   └─ useEditSettingsPersistence      ← bridge layer, own state (isReady)
      └─ useGenerationEditSettings    ← domain wrapper, own state via updateField/Fields
         └─ useAutoSaveSettings       ← reducer with 4 action types, plus 2 load hooks
            └─ useReactQueryModeLoad + useCustomModeLoad   ← both wired with effects
   └─ useUpscale                      ← its own state
   └─ useLoraManager                  ← its own state
```

Every mount:
- useAutoSaveSettings dispatches `LOAD_STARTED` → 1 render
- React Query returns data → `LOAD_RESOLVED` → 1 render
- useEditSettingsPersistence's `isReady` flips → 1 render
- useEditSettingsPersistence's init effect fires `initializeFromLastUsed` → another dispatch → 1 render
- lastUsed DB sync fires → another render
- useUpscale's `setActiveVariant` init → 1 render
- useLoraManager's defaults-apply effect → 1 render

Each of those gets multiplied by the fact that each layer's return object wasn't memoized (I fixed three, but there are effect-triggered state updates that happen independently of memoization). Even fully memoized, you'd still see 7–10 renders on mount from *real* state transitions, not false references.

**Structural smells specifically**:

1. **"Initialize in effect" pattern everywhere**. `useEditSettingsPersistence.ts:118-131`, `useAutoSaveSettings.ts` load effects, `useLastUsedEditSettings.ts:123-146` — every layer has an effect that runs on mount and does a `setState`. These should be `useLayoutEffect` + bailing on no-change, or done at `useState` init time (derivable from props).

2. **Multiple sources of truth for the same value**. `editMode` lives in `lastUsed` (ref + localStorage + DB), in `generationSettings.settings` (reducer state), and in `effectiveSettings` (memo). A write fans out to all three. A read blends all three. This isn't the unstable-ref issue — it's genuine cross-store synchronization.

3. **React Query as the ground truth of state machines**. Every React Query refetch → new data reference → effect → dispatch → render. React Query is fine for "fetch data"; it's structurally bad as the trigger for reducer transitions. The layer between (`useReactQueryModeLoad`) is a lot of code trying to paper over this.

4. **Hook-shaped services**. `useEditSettingsPersistence` is a 350-line hook that's really three services (local UI state, last-used mirror, per-generation persistence) glued together. It re-renders whenever any of the three changes, even when a consumer only cares about one.

5. **The Select is a victim, not the problem**. Base UI Select opens on pointerdown and uses a setTimeout microtask to mount the popup portal. During that microtask, React is still committing the render storm. By the time the click event fires (1-2ms later), the popup DOM doesn't exist yet → Base UI's outside-click handler sees "click outside" → closes.

**What would actually fix this**:
- **Short-term escape hatch**: just use a native `<select>` for the model dropdown. It's 5 minutes, and the render storm stops breaking it. Not pretty, but functional.
- **Medium-term**: replace `useEditSettingsPersistence` + `useGenerationEditSettings` + the last-used hook with a single `EditSettingsStore` object (Zustand / Jotai / useSyncExternalStore). Consumers subscribe to the fields they read. A render in one consumer doesn't ripple to siblings. Mount-time loads happen once, not layered.
- **Long-term**: the "hook-as-service" pattern in this codebase is the pit of success for React re-render bugs. Moving cross-cutting state (persisted settings, tool config, shot settings) to stores instead of hook chains would kill this class of bug permanently.

So yes — we're fighting the architecture. Every fix I ship works but only removes one of many firing paths. The Select will keep flashing closed on any future change that adds another state transition somewhere upstream.

Want me to do the native `<select>` escape hatch so you're unblocked today? The store-based refactor is a real project, not a patch.

> DEVELOPER

Any downsides to the long-term refactor? Assuming we're happy with churn

> AGENT

Real downsides, ranked by how much they actually bite:

**1. Scoped state becomes awkward.** Per-generation settings, per-shot settings — these are naturally "the current entity's data," not global. Stores want to be singletons. You end up either:
- One store with an `entityId` slice (easy to forget to scope selectors, leaks between entities).
- A store-factory pattern with providers (you just re-invented hook chains, with worse DX).

Neither is as clean as `useEditSettingsPersistence(generationId)` reads. The hook-as-service pattern exists because **the settings ARE entity-scoped**. A store refactor has to address this or it'll be worse.

**2. "Why isn't my component re-rendering?" becomes a new bug class.** With stores, re-renders come from selector equality. `useStore(s => s.settings)` re-renders when `settings` reference changes. `useStore(s => s.settings.prompt, shallow)` is stable. Wrong equality function = stale UI. This is the opposite of today's "too many renders" but equally hard to debug, and the failure mode is silent (wrong data on screen) instead of loud (flashing Select).

**3. Testing shifts from "wrap in provider" to "mock the store."** More test surface for integration tests. Harder to test store-internal invariants vs UI concerns.

**4. Lose React's natural lifecycle for some work.** Today, when the lightbox unmounts, hooks clean up automatically. Store-based state survives. You have to manually reset/dispose on entity change — easy to leak stale state (old generation's prompt shown for the new one).

**5. Migration surface is bigger than it looks.** `useAutoSaveSettings` has ~15 callers across the repo, not just media-lightbox. `useToolSettings` has more. Changing the bottom of the stack ripples through every tool. Can be done incrementally (write store alongside, migrate one caller at a time) but it's weeks, not days.

**6. React Query's role gets awkward.** Today, persistence writes go through React Query's invalidation system to keep cached reads fresh. A store has to either (a) still use React Query under the hood for the DB part (two layers of state), or (b) replace it (loses optimistic updates, window-focus refetch, dedup). Neither is free.

**7. Library choice is political.** Zustand, Jotai, Valtio, useSyncExternalStore + custom — each has a religion. Team needs to commit. Wrong pick = another refactor in 18 months.

**8. Bundle size is not a concern.** Zustand is ~1KB. Real but negligible.

**9. The thing a store DOESN'T fix**: if the real problem is that on mount you fire 7 legitimate state transitions in sequence (load → resolve → init-last-used → apply-last-used → ready), you still fire those through a store. The render count goes down because consumers scope to specific fields, but the store itself still does the work. You need to also collapse the transitions (load settings in one atomic step, not four).

**Honest recommendation**: a store alone is not a silver bullet. The refactor that actually pays off is:
- **Collapse the load sequence**: one action, not four. `settingsLoaded({ db, lastUsed })` computes the final state in one go.
- **Single source of truth per field**: `editMode` lives in one place, not three synchronized mirrors.
- **Store for the subscription layer** (so unrelated components don't re-render on each other's changes).
- **Keep React Query for fetches**, feed its data into the store on settle.

That combo fixes the class of bug. Store without the other two changes just moves the pain around.

> AGENT

Zooming out, there are probably 4–5 other places in this codebase with the exact same structural pattern. The value of Zustand isn't picking off one subsystem — it's noticing where the codebase has **"half a store already, built from hooks and providers."**

## Places where this pattern already exists (implicitly)

**1. `useAutoSaveSettings` is a store pretending to be a hook.**
Phase 3 refactor moved it to `useReducer` with 4 action types. That's literally a Redux reducer. The load/save effects are middleware. Make it a real store and you fix `useGenerationEditSettings`, `useShotSettings`, `useInlineEditState`, `useJoinClipsSettings`, `useCharacterAnimateSettings`, and every tool's settings in one shot. ~15 callers converge.

**2. Video editor timeline state.**
Look at `VideoEditorProvider.tsx`: four nested context providers — `TimelineEditorData`, `TimelineEditorOps`, `TimelineChrome`, `TimelinePlayback`. That split is the symptom of "one context caused too many re-renders, so we split by concern." Textbook store use case. `useTimelineState` is ~300 lines of state-keeping that would be half as long as a store, and timeline components could subscribe to the specific slices they care about (scale, selection, playback) without re-rendering on unrelated changes.

**3. Cross-cutting selection state.**
`GallerySelectionContext`, `LastAffectedShotContext`, `CurrentShotContext`, `ShotAdditionSelectionContext`, selection inside the timeline. All of these are "which thing is the user focused on right now" — global-ish, cross-cutting, change often. Five contexts where there should be one store with slices.

**4. Panes / chrome state.**
`PanesContext` tracks which panes are open, locked, widths. Every component inside a pane subscribes to the whole thing and re-renders on any change. Classic store territory.

**5. Realtime event stream.**
`RealtimeProvider` broadcasts task updates. Every consumer re-renders on every event, even if only interested in one task's status. A store with selectors solves this cleanly — `useStore(s => s.tasks[myTaskId]?.status)` re-renders only on that task.

## The intersection

The deep issue isn't any one subsystem — it's that **this codebase uses React context as a pub-sub channel for high-frequency data**. Context isn't that. Context re-renders all consumers on any value change. For settings, selection, realtime events — anything that changes more than once per user action — you want a subscription store.

Signals of this pattern throughout the repo:
- Any `...Context` that wraps a `useMemo` of 15+ fields.
- Any component that subscribes to a big context but only reads two fields.
- Any hook chain where layer N's only job is memoizing layer N-1's output.
- "Split into sub-contexts to reduce re-renders" (you already did this for `ImageEditContext` → `ImageEditCanvasContext` / `ImageEditFormContext` / `ImageEditStatusContext`). That split is a workaround for context-as-pubsub. A store wouldn't need it.

## Where it does NOT belong

- **Forms and transient UI state** (open/closed, hover, focus) → local `useState` always wins.
- **Server data** → keep React Query. Don't replicate server state in the store; feed it as an input.
- **Route state** → React Router.
- **One-shot component-local refs** → `useRef`.

## What a realistic migration looks like

Not one big PR. One domain at a time, in order of pain:

1. **Settings cascade** (highest ROI). One store. `useAutoSaveSettings` becomes `useSettingsStore(selector)`. The cascading resolution (defaults → user → project → shot) becomes store logic, not hook composition. Fixes the render storms we've been chasing.
2. **Selection**. Collapse the 5 selection contexts into one store with slices. No re-render cascade across the gallery when the timeline selects something.
3. **Timeline editor state**. Single store, consumers subscribe to `scale` / `selectedClipId` / etc. Deletes the 4-provider split.
4. **Realtime task events**. Store with per-task slices. Stops updating every consumer on every event.

Panes, chrome state, current-shot state — opportunistic; migrate only when they cause observable issues.

## Bigger-picture win

If this migration happens, you also get:
- **The modal focus bug class dies structurally** — render storms are the reason Base UI overlays unmount mid-open. No storm = overlays stay mounted = focus traps behave.
- **The "memoize everything" discipline relaxes**. Consumers subscribe to specific fields; unstable parent objects don't cascade. New code stops breaking existing performance.
- **"Why isn't my component re-rendering" becomes a simpler debug loop** (selector equality) instead of the current "what effect fired what state update in what order."
- **The useReducer→reducer→dispatch Phase 3 work isn't wasted** — it's 80% of what becomes the store action layer.

## Honest counterpoint

This is a 4–6 week project, done carefully. If the team's headcount is small and the business is moving, "do nothing + patch render bugs as they appear" is a defensible path for 6 more months. The cost of the patching approach is that every new feature risks triggering a new cascade, and onboarding new engineers to this codebase is harder because the state management is implicit in 30 hook chains.

So: yes, this intersects with a lot. If you ever consider a state-management overhaul, the list above is your scope. If you don't, `useEditSettingsPersistence` will keep being a place where subtle bugs appear.

> AGENT

Aggressive 2-week plan. Target: kill the render storm class of bugs structurally, not patch-by-patch. I'd divide it into three atomic migrations, each shippable on its own.

## Tech pick (day 0, 30 min)

**Zustand.** Reasons:
- 1KB, proven, React 18 story is clean (`useSyncExternalStore` underneath).
- Middleware for persistence, devtools, immer if you want.
- Scoped-per-entity is natural: one store, `entities[id]` slice, selectors scope reads.
- Migration path doesn't require touching every caller at once — existing hooks stay, internals swap.

Skip Jotai (atoms-first is correct but the cognitive load slows migration) and Valtio (mutable proxies are off-brand for React). Don't roll your own with `useSyncExternalStore` — Zustand already did it right.

## Week 1: Settings store (biggest ROI)

This alone fixes the Model Select / textarea bug class structurally.

### Day 1 — Foundation
- Stand up `src/shared/state/` with:
  - `createEntityStore<T>()` factory: one store, keyed by `entityId`, with `load`/`update`/`save`/`flush` actions.
  - Persistence middleware: writes to Supabase via the existing service layer (keep React Query as the fetcher; the store subscribes to it on data arrival).
  - TypeScript strictness at the boundary. Fields declared once, consumers get typed selectors.
- One example store: port `useJoinClipsSettings` (smallest caller, 5 fields). Validate the shape.

### Day 2–3 — Core settings store
- Replace `useAutoSaveSettings` internals with a single store. Keep the hook signature — consumers don't change. The hook becomes `function useAutoSaveSettings<T>(opts) { useMemo → selector → store }`.
- **Collapse the mount-time load sequence into one atomic action.** Today: `LOAD_STARTED` → React Query resolves → `LOAD_RESOLVED` → `initializeFromLastUsed` → save-back. Make it one `bootstrapEntity({ db, lastUsed })` that computes the final state in one pass. **This is what actually stops the storm** — the memoization fixes only stop false cascades, the collapsed load stops legitimate ones.
- Keep `hasPendingFor` / edit-version protection — just move them into the store.
- Delete `useDebouncedSettingsSave` as a separate hook; absorb into the store.

### Day 4 — Migrate the loud callers
- `useShotSettings`, `useEditSettingsPersistence`, `useGenerationEditSettings`, `useInlineEditState`.
- Each becomes a thin selector wrapper over the store. No behavior change visible to panels.
- Render storm in media-lightbox drops from 20 → 1–2. Model Select works. Textarea accepts typing.
- Delete `useLastUsedEditSettings` (its ref-based pseudo-state becomes a real store slice).

### Day 5 — Delete dead code + fix tests
- `autoSaveSettingsHelpers.ts`, `autoSaveSettingsLoaders.ts`, the useReducer — all unnecessary once the store owns the state machine.
- `useEditModePanelState` can drop its "hybrid props/context" shape — consumers just use the store directly via selectors.
- Update tests. Delete the 400 lines of `InlineEditView.test.tsx` that test implementation details; keep the user-behavior tests.

**End of week 1**: ~2000 lines deleted, ~800 added. Storm fixed. Phase 1/2/3 of the megaplan becomes a clean backward-compatible refactor in retrospect.

## Week 2: Selection store + timeline state

### Day 6–7 — Unified selection store
Collapse `GallerySelectionContext`, `LastAffectedShotContext`, `CurrentShotContext`, `ShotAdditionSelectionContext`, and the timeline's internal selection into one store with slices:

```
selection: {
  gallery: { ids: [], last: null }
  timeline: { clipIds: [], trackId: null, primary: null }
  shot: { current: null, lastAffected: null }
}
```

Cross-cutting behaviors that required `useEffect` chains today become single actions:
- "Clicking gallery item deselects timeline" → one dispatch.
- "Creating a shot sets lastAffected" → one dispatch.

Kill the useEffect-driven sync between contexts. That sync itself was a re-render source.

Components subscribe to specific slices. Touching `selection.shot` doesn't re-render the timeline.

### Day 8–9 — Timeline editor state
This is the big one. Today's four providers (`TimelineEditorData`, `Ops`, `Chrome`, `Playback`) merge into one store. Consumers subscribe to what they need:

```ts
const scale = useTimelineStore(s => s.scale)
const selectedClipId = useTimelineStore(s => s.selectedClipId)
```

Aggressive angles:
- **Refs-for-stability workarounds die**. `editorRef.current` patterns scattered through `VideoEditorProvider.tsx` — the store is always latest, no ref dance.
- **`useTimelineState.ts` is ~300 lines that become ~150**. Half of it is currently memo plumbing, not logic.
- **The Ops/Data split was a workaround for context-as-pubsub**. Store subscription makes it moot.

### Day 10 — Consolidation + docs
- Write a 1-page "how state lives in this codebase now" doc in `docs/structure_detail/`.
- Add a brief ESLint rule or convention: context values >10 fields must be a store, not a context.
- Kill stale hooks now made irrelevant.
- Open follow-up issues for realtime + panes migrations (not in this 2 weeks).

## Rules during the sprint

1. **One PR per atomic migration.** Foundation → core store → settings callers → selection store → timeline store. Each PR reverts cleanly. No multi-day branches.
2. **Keep hook names at the API boundary.** `useShotSettings(id)` stays; only its implementation swaps. Migration done "from underneath." No consumer file changes in the settings migration.
3. **Don't replace React Query.** Store subscribes to RQ data on arrival via the existing `useToolSettings` hook. Two-way binding is wrong; one-way (RQ → store) is right.
4. **Delete aggressively.** If a helper hook exists only to paper over the old problem, it goes. `useDebouncedSettingsSave`, `autoSaveSettingsHelpers`, `autoSaveSettingsLoaders`, the `isReady` state in `useEditSettingsPersistence`, `hasInitializedRef` dance — all disappear.
5. **No dev-time performance regressions allowed.** Add a render counter to `LightboxShell`, `TimelineCanvas`, and one timeline track row in dev mode. If they go up, the migration regressed.
6. **TypeScript strict from day one.** Store actions should be exhaustive unions; selectors should infer precisely. This is your chance to enforce types in places `any` leaked.

## Realistic expectations

**Will definitely happen in 2 weeks**: Settings store shipped and adopted. Render storm fixed. Selection store shipped. Model Select works. Textarea works. ~3000 lines of memo/ref plumbing deleted.

**Might slip**: Full timeline migration (it's the most tangled). If slipping, stop at "store created, half the consumers migrated, rest continue using context temporarily." The store can coexist with context during migration.

**Won't happen**: Realtime store, panes store, `ImageEditContext` split reunification, full test rewrite. Those are weeks 3–6.

## Biggest risk

The timeline migration is the hairiest. `useTimelineState.ts` + its sub-hooks (`useClipDrag`, `useClipResizeGesture`, `useAssetManagement`, `useExternalDrop`, `useTimelinePersistence`, `usePollSync`) are interdependent, and the existing ref-based coordination is subtle. Two days is tight. If aggressive pays off here, great. If not, land settings + selection in week 1, and spend week 2 doing just the timeline Data/Ops merge cleanly, leaving playback/chrome alone.

## The one question I'd ask before starting

Does the team have appetite to keep Zustand forever? This is a one-way door at the codebase level. Once the settings store is in and 15 callers depend on it, you can't ergonomically swap libraries in a year. If "yes, we commit," proceed aggressively. If "maybe, we'll see" — don't start. Half-migrated state management is worse than all-hooks or all-store.

> DEVELOPER

ANd what after this?

> AGENT

After the 2-week sprint, I'd think in three bands: **weeks 3–4** (finish the job the sprint started), **months 2–3** (apply the pattern elsewhere), **month 4+** (structural cleanup that was previously impossible).

## Weeks 3–4: Close the gaps the sprint opened

The sprint will reveal things that weren't obvious before. Expect to discover:

**1. Realtime events store.** `RealtimeProvider` pushes task updates through context. Every listener re-renders on every event. Once the subscription pattern is proven by the settings/timeline work, this is a half-day port — `useTaskStatus(taskId)` becomes `useRealtimeStore(s => s.tasks[taskId]?.status)`. Fixes the "gallery flickers on every backend event" class.

**2. Modal / overlay registry.** The original focus-trap bug (textarea can't type, Select flashes closed) happens because ~30 Base UI overlays each manage their own body-lock independently. Build one `useOverlayStack()` primitive:
- Register on mount (with `open` state tracked in the stack).
- Body `pointer-events: none` only when stack is non-empty AND outermost is `modal: true`.
- Focus restoration centralized.
- Wrap `<Dialog>`, `<Popover>`, `<Select>`, `<Menu>` in thin in-house components that use the stack.

This kills the entire class of "overlay unmounts while open leaves body locked" bugs — structurally, not by careful patching per-file. The ESLint rule we added becomes unnecessary.

**3. Tool settings consolidation.** Each tool's settings hook is now a selector over the same store pattern. Unify them — not their data, but their scaffold. `createToolSettingsStore<T>({ tool, defaults, resolve })` replaces `useShotSettings`, `useCharacterAnimateSettings`, `useJoinClipsSettings`, etc. One implementation, 15 instantiations. Deletes hundreds of duplicated lines.

**4. Delete the context-split workarounds.** `ImageEditContext` was split into Canvas/Form/Status because a single context was re-rendering too much. With a store, the split is unnecessary. Reunify. Less indirection, fewer files to navigate.

**5. Kill `useReactQueryModeLoad` / `useCustomModeLoad`.** Once the store owns state, the two "modes" for load collapse into one: RQ fetches → store receives. The branching in `autoSaveSettingsLoaders.ts` goes away.

## Months 2–3: Extend the pattern to remaining sharp edges

**6. Panes store.** Medium priority because panes don't cause render storms — they just accumulate coupling. Clean port. Delete `PanesContext`.

**7. Per-shot video-travel state migration.** `VideoTravelSettingsProvider` is the biggest remaining hook-as-service. Port its 12 sub-hooks (`usePromptSettings`, `useMotionSettings`, `useGenerationModeSettings`, etc.) to selectors over a single VideoTravel store. This is where the `[ModeDebug]` spam originated — the logs we saw in that earlier capture disappear entirely.

**8. Task creation / queue state.** Task creation goes through `settingsWriteQueue.ts` + ad-hoc hooks. This has the same shape as settings: "entity-scoped mutable state with debounced persistence." Port to the same store factory you built in the sprint.

**9. Performance budgets in dev.** Add a tiny dev-only hook: `useRenderBudget('ImageLightbox', 5)`. Warns in console if component exceeds expected renders per interaction. Catches regressions before they ship. This is what kept biting you during this debugging session — you had no signal until users reported "can't type."

**10. Test suite triage.** The full suite has ~36 pre-existing failures from unrelated areas (travel-between-images, timeline tests). Bisect against `main`, fix or delete. Target: clean green suite, so future regressions are visible.

## Month 4+: Things that only become possible after the above

**11. Tool abstraction.** Once each tool's state is a store and each tool's settings is a standard shape, the concept of a "tool" can become first-class. `defineTool({ id, settings, components, routes })` replaces the scattered tool-registration logic. New tools are one file.

**12. Edit-pipeline consolidation.** `useInpainting` + `useMagicEditMode` + `useRepositionMode` + `useImg2ImgMode` + `useUpscale` all share a shape: "take media, take settings, submit a task." They currently live as ~5 hooks with overlapping concerns in `useImageEditOrchestrator`. Extract to a common `EditMode` interface + dispatch table. The per-mode panel split you already did (TextEditPanel, InpaintPanel, etc.) becomes genuinely modular — one panel + one edit-mode runner + one entry in a dispatch table to add a new mode.

**13. Agent / AI feature surfaces.** Agents (timeline agent, effect creator, voice input) all manipulate store state. Once state is observable, agents can subscribe and react rather than getting wired through a tangle of bridge hooks (`AgentChatBridgeRegistration` etc.). Single "agent state adapter" that projects the store into an LLM-friendly context.

**14. Route-level code splitting.** Right now everything is bundled together; `AppProviders` wraps a huge provider tree at root. Once stores replace context for the cross-cutting stuff, route-level stores let you code-split by tool. User who only opens image-generation doesn't load video-editor state.

**15. Server components / loaders.** If Next/TanStack Router is ever on the table, the store-based architecture is a much better starting point for server-rendered state. Today's hook chains can't do that — they depend on client-only effects.

## What shouldn't make it onto this list

A few things that look tempting but aren't worth the churn:
- **Replacing shadcn/Base UI**. The library works. The problem is our usage patterns, not the lib.
- **Moving to Next.js**. Vite + React Router is fine. Churn-to-value ratio is bad.
- **Redux or Redux Toolkit**. Zustand is the right size; RTK adds ceremony without new power for this codebase.
- **A generic "state machine" library (XState etc.)**. The state in this app is tree-shaped, not graph-shaped. Overkill.

## The big-picture destination

After ~4 months of this, the codebase's mental model becomes:
- **Server state** = React Query.
- **Shared client state** = a handful of Zustand stores (settings, selection, timeline, realtime, panes).
- **Local UI state** = `useState`/`useRef`, unapologetically.
- **Cross-component behavior** = store actions, not effect chains.
- **Overlays** = a shared stack primitive with a single body-lock owner.

The thing that matters: **"why is this component rendering?" becomes answerable in seconds**. Today it's a multi-hour debug session per incident. That velocity delta compounds on every feature.

## The one discipline to hold

Aggressive sprints leave entropy unless followed by aggressive deletion. For every store/primitive added, delete the predecessor the same PR. Don't let the old hooks linger as "backup." Within 2 months the codebase should be net-smaller, not larger.

> DEVELOPER

Any downsides ot this approach?

> AGENT

Real ones, worth thinking through before committing:

**1. Scope creep is almost guaranteed.** Once you start seeing the shape clearly, every other subsystem will look like it wants the same treatment. The list I wrote is already ambitious; your brain will add to it. Two weeks of sprint becomes four becomes "Q2 is rebuilding state management." Budget discipline matters more than ambition.

**2. It reveals pre-existing rot you can't un-see.** The sprint will surface assumptions baked into ad-hoc hooks — "oh, `useShotSettings` was silently depending on `useToolSettings` returning a stale reference when X," etc. You'll either have to fix those (scope explosion) or preserve the quirk deliberately in the new store (technical debt transfer). Neither feels good.

**3. It trades one bug class for another.** Today's bugs: "too many renders, can't-type-in-textarea, flashing Select." Post-migration bugs: "stale selector equality, store update happened but component didn't re-render, consumer reading a slice that was reset by another action." These are quieter and harder to reproduce. You spend less time firefighting, more time on subtle correctness issues.

**4. Cross-store coordination is still hard.** Zustand doesn't solve "when selection changes, save settings; when settings save, refetch tasks." That glue still has to live somewhere. Effect chains in components become action chains in stores — better, but not free. Easy to end up with a new kind of spaghetti if you're not careful.

**5. React Query ↔ store sync is a new source of truth problem.** Data lives in RQ cache and in the store. Which one is authoritative during a write? What happens when RQ invalidates but the store has an uncommitted edit? You have to design this explicitly. `useAutoSaveSettings` today has the same problem (`pendingSettingsRef`, edit-version checks) — that logic doesn't vanish, it moves into the store. Sometimes the hook form was actually doing a useful job.

**6. Test surface shifts.** Tests that currently wrap components in providers will wrap them in store mocks. Unit tests of hooks become unit tests of selectors + actions. The delta is probably 30% of your existing test files need updating. If your test culture is shaky, migration makes coverage worse before it gets better.

**7. New engineer onboarding gets harder, not easier, short-term.** "Read a hook, follow its types" is universal React knowledge. "Read a Zustand store, understand this codebase's entity-scoping convention, know which store owns what" is local knowledge. Breaks even at ~3 months, positive after 6. Painful in the meantime if you're hiring.

**8. Zustand is a long-term commitment you can't easily exit.** Once 15+ stores depend on its selector model, middleware, and `create()` patterns, swapping to a new library is a year of work. React 19's `use` + compiler may change what's idiomatic; if you pick Zustand now and React's native primitives eat its lunch in 2 years, you've got a "legacy state library" situation. Mitigated but not eliminated by keeping your store factory thin and under your control.

**9. Feature velocity hits during migration.** The 2-week sprint ships feature work at near-zero. Month 2–3 slows feature work by ~30% as PRs conflict with migration work. If there's a deadline looming (product launch, investor demo, customer SLA), this is risky. Teams underestimate this consistently.

**10. Half-done migrations are worse than either endpoint.** If the sprint lands but months 2–3 get deprioritized, you're left with "some things are stores, some are hooks" — engineers have to know which is which for every feature. This happens in most migrations. Need a real commitment to finish, not just start.

**11. Stores obscure call graphs.** Today, `useShotSettings(id)` → you can follow the hook chain and see what it reads. With stores, `useStore(s => s.shots[id].settings)` — you know the shape but not who writes to it. Debugging "why did this value change" becomes grep-for-action rather than read-the-hook. Tools (Redux DevTools, Zustand devtools) help but add ceremony.

**12. Overlay stack primitive is optimistic scope.** I listed it as a months-2-3 win. It's also the single hardest piece, because it requires understanding Base UI's internal focus/body-lock lifecycle in detail. Base UI is less documented than Radix. Might take longer than budgeted. Could be its own project.

**13. The motivating bug might have a smaller fix.** The Model Select closes instantly because of render storms. Maybe the storm has a 1-line root cause we haven't found yet — some specific effect with wrong deps somewhere in `useImageLightboxEnvironment`'s transitive call graph. If so, a precision fix is 1 day vs 2 weeks. I don't think it does (we chased three unstable hooks + the dimensions loop + the defaults ref, and the storm remains), but I can't rule it out without more digging.

**14. Scoped-per-entity state is Zustand's least-natural use case.** The current app is fundamentally about "the current generation's prompt," "the current shot's settings," "the current timeline's clips." Jotai's atom-per-entity model would be cleaner. Zustand with `entities[id]` works but you'll occasionally fight the ergonomics. I recommended Zustand for migration speed, not fit. If you're exceptionally talented and happy with aggressive churn, Jotai is probably the better pick and worth a day reconsidering.

**15. "The codebase is consistent" was actually a strength.** Right now, every settings hook looks the same shape. Every context is memoized the same way. A new engineer can pattern-match. Post-migration, there's a period where patterns diverge before they reconverge. Consistency is a feature; this breaks it deliberately.

---

**The honest summary**: this is correct architecture and the bugs that motivate it are real. The downsides are mostly about execution risk and opportunity cost, not "bad idea." The way to de-risk most of them:

- **Get explicit team commitment upfront.** Not "sounds good" — "yes we will finish this, here's the 4-month milestone plan signed off."
- **Decide on Zustand vs Jotai on day 1 and don't revisit.** The switching cost 6 months in is punishing.
- **Write the "state architecture" doc on day 2**, before any code. If you can't explain where state lives in one page, you're not ready to refactor. If you can, that doc becomes the thing new engineers read.
- **Define "done" concretely.** "All 15 settings hooks migrated, all context providers <10 fields, overlay stack shipped, panes migrated." Not "cleaner state."
- **Keep a kill switch.** If at week 3 the team is miserable and product is bleeding, revert the sprint PR (one PR, atomic = easy), accept the render storms, and patch per-incident. Don't sunk-cost your way through.

If you accept all of the above and still want to go, I'd bet on success. The list of downsides is long but none are fatal. The biggest real risk is **not finishing** — everything else is manageable.

#!/bin/bash
# Manually spawn a GPU worker or manage existing ones.
#
# Usage:
#   worker-spawn.sh                    # Spawn a new worker
#   worker-spawn.sh list               # List active workers
#   worker-spawn.sh status <worker_id> # Check specific worker
#   worker-spawn.sh terminate <id>     # Terminate specific worker

set -e

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
ORCH_DIR="$SCRIPT_DIR/../reigh-worker-orchestrator"

if [ ! -d "$ORCH_DIR" ]; then
    echo "Error: reigh-worker-orchestrator not found at $ORCH_DIR"
    exit 1
fi

cd "$ORCH_DIR"

ACTION="${1:-spawn}"

case "$ACTION" in
    list|status|spawn|terminate)
        shift 2>/dev/null || true
        PYENV_VERSION=3.11.11 python scripts/spawn_gpu.py "$ACTION" "$@"
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Usage: worker-spawn.sh [spawn|list|status|terminate] [args...]"
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

> AGENT

Yes, `platform.openai.com/api-keys` is the right place — but let me clarify because there's a real distinction that trips people up:

**Codex CLI has two auth modes:**

1. **ChatGPT subscription** (Plus/Pro/Team) — you run `codex login` and it OAuths through your ChatGPT account. Usage is bundled into your subscription (no per-token billing). Cheapest if you already have ChatGPT Pro ($200/mo covers heavy usage) or Plus ($20/mo with daily limits).

2. **OpenAI API key** (pay-per-token) — from `platform.openai.com/api-keys`. Same place developers get keys for `openai` SDK calls. Codex bills against that account per token of input/output. No subscription needed; separate billing from ChatGPT.

**For a headless Railway container, option 2 is the only real choice** — OAuth needs a browser, which we don't have on the remote.

So: yes, **platform.openai.com/api-keys** is correct for what we're doing.

Two gotchas to know:

- **The `platform.openai.com` account is separate from your ChatGPT account** (even though you can sign in with the same email). Your ChatGPT Plus subscription does NOT give you free platform.openai.com API credits — that's a common surprise. You'll start with $0 credit and need to add payment info.
- **You need at least ~$5 of credit loaded** before the key works. Go to https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/billing/overview → add a payment method → buy credits.

If you'd rather not deal with a separate billing surface and you have ChatGPT Pro ($200/mo), there's a workaround: we can do `codex login` interactively on your laptop, then copy `~/.codex/auth.json` over to the container. Less clean (OAuth tokens expire and re-auth needs a browser) but avoids paying OpenAI twice. Your call — want to do the API-key route or the subscription-copy route?

Confirmed from your own machine: codex stores the key under the field literally named **`OPENAI_API_KEY`** in `~/.codex/auth.json`. That's the same key type you get at `platform.openai.com/api-keys`.

**So:**
- "Codex API key" = "OpenAI API key" — same thing, just different branding context.
- Get it at **https://platform.openai.com/api-keys**.
- Format: `sk-proj-...` or `sk-...`.

If you've seen something online calling it a "Codex key" separately, that's older marketing — in 2021–2022 there was a deprecated model named `code-davinci` (sometimes called "Codex"). The new Codex CLI (2025) uses regular OpenAI API keys.

Create src/shared/state/createEntityStore.ts — a generic Zustand store factory for entity-scoped settings.\n   - Takes a default value shape T, a load fn, a save fn, an entity type label.\n   - Returns a store with actions: bootstrapEntity({ entityId, db, lastUsed }), updateField, updateFields, updateTextField (deferred save), flushTextFields, revert, reset.\n   - State shape: { entityId, status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'ready' | 'saving' | 'error', settings: T, loadedSettings: T, error: Error | null, hasPersistedData: boolean, pendingEntityId: string | null, pendingSettings: T | null, editVersion: number }.\n   - One atomic bootstrap action that computes the final state from db + lastUsed in a single dispatch (not four sequential transitions).\n   - Preserve the pending-text-field protection from useDebouncedSettingsSave (tracks user edits while a load is in flight so refetches don't stomp typing).\n\n2. Yep — "zoo stands" = Zustand. Here's the tight version of the 2-week aggressive plan we laid out:

## Week 1 — Settings store (biggest ROI, fixes the current bug class)

**Day 1 — Foundation**
- `src/shared/state/createEntityStore.ts`: generic Zustand factory (bootstrap/update/flush/revert/reset actions).
- Validate shape by porting the smallest caller (`useJoinClipsSettings`, 5 fields).

**Day 2–3 — Core store**
- Replace `useAutoSaveSettings` internals with the store. Keep the hook signature — no consumer changes.
- **Collapse the mount-time load sequence into one atomic `bootstrapEntity({ db, lastUsed })` action.** Today: 4 sequential state transitions (LOAD_STARTED → resolved → init-last-used → ready). Tomorrow: one.
- Absorb `useDebouncedSettingsSave` (pending tracking, edit versioning) into the store.

**Day 4 — Migrate loud callers**
`useShotSettings`, `useEditSettingsPersistence`, `useGenerationEditSettings`, `useInlineEditState` become selector wrappers. **Render storm dies** — Model Select works, textarea accepts typing, visible proof.

**Day 5 — Delete dead code**
`autoSaveSettingsHelpers.ts`, `autoSaveSettingsLoaders.ts`, the reducer, `useLastUsedEditSettings`'s ref-as-state, `hasInitializedRef`/`isReady` dance. Tests updated; implementation-detail ones deleted. End week 1: ~2000 lines deleted, ~800 added.

## Week 2 — Selection + timeline

**Day 6–7 — Unified selection store**
Collapse `GallerySelectionContext`, `LastAffectedShotContext`, `CurrentShotContext`, `ShotAdditionSelectionContext`, and timeline selection into one store with slices. Cross-cutting behaviors ("click gallery → deselect timeline") become one dispatch instead of effect-chain glue.

**Day 8–9 — Timeline editor state**
Merge the 4 context providers (`TimelineEditorData`, `Ops`, `Chrome`, `Playback`) into one store. `editorRef.current` workarounds in `VideoEditorProvider.tsx` die. `useTimelineState.ts` goes from ~300 lines to ~150.

**Day 10 — Consolidation**
One-page "how state lives now" doc. ESLint rule: contexts >10 fields must be a store. Delete stragglers. Open follow-up issues (realtime, panes) for weeks 3–4.

## Non-negotiable rules

1. **One PR per atomic migration.** Reverts cleanly.
2. **Hook names stay at the API boundary.** Internals swap, consumers untouched.
3. **Don't replace React Query.** Store subscribes to RQ; RQ fetches server state.
4. **Delete aggressively.** Predecessor removed in the same PR that adds the successor.
5. **No dev-time perf regressions.** Render counter on `LightboxShell`, `TimelineCanvas`, one timeline row. If they go up, revert.
6. **TypeScript strict throughout.**

## What the current megaplan run is scoped to

Just Week 1 (the settings store). I deliberately kept the idea tight — foundation + core rewrite + four caller migrations + deletion sweep. Selection store and timeline store are separate megaplans (week 2 items), to ship as separate PRs.

That matches the "one PR per atomic migration" discipline. If you want the whole 2 weeks in one megaplan run I can re-scope it, but I'd recommend not — week 1 is already ambitious for one execute pass, and the selection/timeline work benefits from reviewing week 1's shape first.

Auto-approve is on — megaplan will now run prep → plan → critique → gate → finalize → **execute** → review without stopping.

Now, about preservation — **honest answer: not yet.** Here's the state:

Currently, **everything the agent writes (code, megaplan artifacts, tmux state) lives only on the container's ephemeral filesystem**. Railway containers get wiped and re-created on:
- Redeploy (including when we change env vars)
- Auto-restart from crash
- Scale-down events
- Underlying infrastructure moves

The entrypoint re-clones the repo from GitHub on every restart, which means **any uncommitted code changes codex produces will be erased** if the container restarts mid-run. The megaplan state files under `.megaplan/plans/` would go with them.

Two fixes, let me do both now:

1. **Persistent volume** — Railway supports volumes. Mount one at `/workspace` so the filesystem survives restarts.
2. **Push to GitHub after commits** — need your `GITHUB_TOKEN` so codex can `git push` its work to a branch. Volume + pushes gives durability even if Railway nukes the container entirely.

Here's the situation — I need a decision from you before I touch anything mid-run:

**Current reality**: container is ephemeral, the plan state is on its ephemeral disk, prep is ~90 seconds in.

**Adding a volume right now = interrupt the plan**. Railway attaches volumes by redeploy, which wipes the filesystem (the volume is empty initially), which kills the current prep. You'd lose ~2 minutes of prep work and I'd re-init the plan fresh.

**Three paths, pick one:**

**A. Just push to GitHub (cleanest, requires token)**
Add a `GITHUB_TOKEN`, codex commits + pushes to a branch after each migration PR. Container can die anytime after that — commits survive on GitHub. No volume needed. Works with the current in-flight prep; no restart.

**B. Add a volume + token (belt + suspenders)**
Interrupt the run, add a volume, restart, re-init, continue. Container state persists across restarts AND commits push to GitHub. Overkill for a 1-day run but bulletproof.

**C. No volume, no token (you accept the risk)**
Container restarts = total loss. Fine if you're watching it actively and plan to finish today. Not fine overnight / multi-day.

**My recommendation: A**. Two-week autonomous run → commits-to-branch is the right durability model anyway (gives you reviewable PRs as it progresses). Volume is a maintenance surface we don't need. Container gets cheap to blow away & restart; nothing important lives only there.

-f /root/.codex/auth.json ]]; then\n  echo \"Authenticating codex with OPENAI_API_KEY\"\n  printf '%s' \"$OPENAI_API_KEY\" | codex login --with-api-key 2>&1 | tail -3 || true\nfi\n\n# Megaplan config — force all phases onto codex + auto-approve on every boot\nif ! command -v megaplan >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n  echo \"Reinstalling megaplan from source...\"\n  pip install --no-cache-dir git+https://github.com/peteromallet/megaplan.git 2>&1 | tail -3\nfi\n\necho \"Configuring megaplan: all phases -> codex, auto_approve=true, robustness=standard\"\nfor phase in plan prep critique revise gate finalize review loop_plan loop_execute; do\n  megaplan config set \"agents.$phase\" codex >/dev/null 2>&1 || true\ndone\nmegaplan config set execution.auto_approve true >/dev/null 2>&1 || true\nmegaplan config set execution.robustness standard >/dev/null 2>&1 || true\n\n# Tiny health server so Railway keeps container alive\npython3 /usr/local/bin/healthserver.py &\nHEALTH_PID=$!\necho \"healthserver.py running as pid $HEALTH_PID\"\n\n# Ensure tmux session 'agent' exists\nif ! > AGENT

Honest audit — most of it is solid, but there are real gaps that matter more when the agent is running autonomously. I'll rank them.

## What's solid
- Motivation ties directly to the bugs we diagnosed. The agent won't get lost on why this is worth doing.
- Zustand is explicitly locked in. No debates mid-run.
- React Query stays as the server-data layer — correct call.
- "Migrate internals, preserve hook signatures" is the right discipline.
- Caller file paths are enumerated. No grep-fishing for scope.
- Deletion list is specific. Prevents "leave it for backup" drift.
- Success criteria has verifiable `MUST`s alongside `SHOULD`s.

## Real gaps for an autonomous run

**1. Day 6–9 is too optimistic.** Selection store collapses 5 contexts in 2 days; timeline store merges 4 contexts + 6 coordinating sub-hooks (`useClipDrag`, `useClipResizeGesture`, `useAssetManagement`, `useExternalDrop`, `useTimelinePersistence`, `usePollSync`) in 2 days. That's the hairiest code in the repo. Realistic: 4–5 days combined. Auto-approve doesn't stop it from rushing and leaving breakage.

**2. "5 separate PRs" vs. one execute run.** The idea says five PRs on five branches. Megaplan's execute phase is one run — it'll likely produce one big commit chain, not five reviewable PRs. Either relax that or the agent will half-follow and confuse itself.

**3. No CI verification gate.** I wrote "typecheck clean + tests pass" but didn't mandate codex actually run them between batches. With auto-approve, it could land broken code and move on.

**4. "Render count ≤ 3"** is a number I picked without measurement. Real baseline might be 4–5. Could fail the MUST for non-bug reasons and cause an infinite rework loop.

**5. Selector equality isn't specified.** Zustand's default is `Object.is`. Slice selectors that return objects need `shallow` or custom equality. Not in the idea. Codex might write selectors that re-render on every store change → undo the whole point.

**6. Overlay focus bug — the motivating symptom — has no test.** MUST says "Select stays open" but there's no existing integration test for that. Codex has no way to auto-verify it beyond typecheck+unit tests.

**7. "Tests pass" vs. 19 pre-existing failing files.** The idea says "match that baseline" but codex may take "tests pass" literally and loop trying to fix unrelated failures.

**8. "Delete aggressively" + auto-approve + no human checkpoint = risk.** Nothing stops codex from deleting a file that turns out to be load-bearing in ways the idea doesn't anticipate (e.g., a consumer in a test file, an edge function, a settings migration).

**9. No token/time budget.** 2 weeks of work through gpt-5.4-high at reasoning=high could cost $200–500+. No cap in the idea.

**10. GITHUB_TOKEN is a classic PAT with broad scope.** Write access to all banodoco repos, not just reigh-app. Already flagged, but worth repeating — if codex goes off-script it could touch the wrong repo.

## What I'd change before letting it run overnight

Ranked by impact:

**A. Add a human checkpoint between week 1 and week 2.** Either split into two megaplans, or pause auto-approve after the week-1 execute phase. This is the single most important change. The settings store migration is achievable; the selection+timeline migrations are genuinely hard and benefit from seeing week 1 land cleanly before continuing.

**B. Require verification between each PR.** Add to the idea: "After each of the 5 migrations lands, run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx vitest run <affected paths>`. If either fails, abort the current batch and report, do not proceed."

**C. Budget cap.** Add "If total execute cost exceeds $150 cumulative, stop and escalate."

**D. Explicit `shallow` selector requirement.** Add to the Zustand section: "All selectors that return objects MUST use `shallow` equality from `zustand/shallow`. Single-value selectors (primitives, refs) use default."

**E. Soft-float the render target.** Change `MUST: ≤ 3 renders` to `MUST: ≤ 5 renders and ≥ 75% reduction from baseline` — tolerates measurement variance.

**F. Finalize as five commits on five branches** —

> DEVELOPER

And it'll definitely persist on that machine?

> AGENT

Partial yes. Let me be precise because it matters:

## What persists across restarts (volume-backed at `/workspace`)
- ✅ Repo files, including any uncommitted changes codex writes
- ✅ Megaplan plan state (`.megaplan/plans/<plan-name>/` — state.json, plan_vN.md, critique, etc.)
- ✅ Megaplan idea file at `/workspace/megaplan-idea-2week.txt`
- ✅ All logs at `/workspace/megaplan-*.log`

## What DOES NOT persist, but gets auto-recreated by the entrypoint on boot
- Codex auth (`/root/.codex/auth.json`) — re-created from `OPENAI_API_KEY` env var on boot
- Codex config (`gpt-5.4` + `reasoning=high`) — written by entrypoint
- Megaplan config (all-codex, auto-approve) — written by entrypoint
- Git credential helper (`GITHUB_TOKEN`) — written by entrypoint
- Tmux session named `agent` — re-created empty

## What DOES NOT persist and is NOT recovered automatically
- **The running megaplan/codex processes**. If the container restarts mid-prep / mid-execute, those processes die. The plan state on disk is intact, but megaplan doesn't auto-resume — someone (me or you) has to run `megaplan <next-step> --plan <name>` to continue from the last checkpoint.
- **Tmux session contents** (scrollback, any manual commands in flight).

## When does a restart happen?
- Code push / redeploy → yes, it restarts
- Setting a new env var → yes, it restarts
- Container crash → Railway restarts it automatically
- Idle / scale-to-zero → Railway hobby plan doesn't actually scale to zero by default; the container stays up unless you `railway down`
- You explicitly run `railway down` → container stops, volume stays attached (not deleted)
- **Deleting the project or volume** → everything gone

## Honest risks
1. **Mid-execute restart = work lost unless committed.** If codex is mid-way through a migration, has written 10 files, and the container restarts, those files ARE preserved (volume) BUT megaplan doesn't know to continue — the plan state says "execute in progress" but no process is running. You'd have to manually re-kick `megaplan execute` and hope the evidence files align. **Mitigation**: codex should commit + push frequently (GITHUB_TOKEN is set, so it can). I should add to the idea an instruction: "Commit and push after each batch completes."
2. **Volume deletion is the only true data loss event.** If you run `railway volume delete` or the project dies, everything goes. Volumes are durable otherwise.
3. **Token expiry.** `OPENAI_API_KEY` doesn't expire but your spending limit might hit. `GITHUB_TOKEN` expires per your PAT settings (classic tokens can be set to "no expiration," fine-grained max 1 year). If GITHUB_TOKEN expires mid-run, push will start failing silently.

## Two improvements I'd make right now

**B. Require codex to commit-and-push after each migration step.** Add to the idea text. Then even volume loss is recoverable via `git clone` from the pushed branch.

> AGENT

Yes — 95% of it is mechanical, and codex can absolutely do it. Here's the breakdown:

**Deterministic parts (no real judgment):**
- Read `next_step` from `megaplan status`, run that phase, repeat.
- If state is `done` or `aborted` → stop.
- If phase fails → retry once with `--fresh`, then escalate.
- After `gate` returns `PROCEED` → `finalize` → `execute` → `review`.
- After `gate` returns `ITERATE` → `revise` → back to `critique` → `gate`.

**Places where judgment-ish calls happen, but codex can follow rules:**
- `gate` returns `ESCALATE` → the canned rules say "ask user" — but with auto-approve we've said "just force-proceed." Codex can do that.
- `revise` loop keeps not converging (score plateaus) → rule: force-proceed after N iterations. Codex can count.
- `execute` makes no forward progress 3 times → escalate to user. Codex can count.
- `review` returns `needs_rework` → loop back to execute. Already a defined rule.

**Truly judgmental (and rare):**
- `gate_escalate` with an ambiguous signal on a high-stakes plan — in practice this is rare at `standard` robustness.

**Two options, pick one:**

**(A) Dumb shell driver** — 10 lines, no cost, no judgment:
```bash
while true; do
  NEXT=$(megaplan status --plan <name> --json | jq -r '.next_step // "none"')
  [[ "$NEXT" == "none" || "$NEXT" == "null" ]] && break
  megaplan "$NEXT" --plan <name> --confirm-destructive || break
done
```
Runs the whole chain end-to-end. No AI in the orchestration loop, just reacts to `next_step`. Handles happy path perfectly. Fails noisily on anything unusual → you intervene.

**(B) Codex as orchestrator** — uses a driver prompt, handles edge cases with actual reasoning:
```bash
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "$(cat /workspace/orchestrator-prompt.txt)" 2>&1 | tee /workspace/orchestrator.log
```
The prompt tells codex: "Drive the plan `<name>` to completion. Run each phase. Handle gate recommendations per these rules. Retry once on failure. Stop on X/Y/Z." Costs tokens but handles escalation gracefully.

**My recommendation: (A) + codex only at execute.** The orchestration loop itself is dumb logic — no reason to burn gpt-5.4-high tokens on running `while` loops. The expensive thinking happens inside each phase (plan, critique, execute), which already uses codex.

Sense-check says **A is fine with 3 guardrails**. Here's the honest audit:

## What requires zero judgment
- Happy-path phase transitions: `prep → plan → critique → gate → finalize → execute → review → done`.
- `gate: PROCEED` → next_step is `finalize`. Run it.
- `gate: ITERATE` → next_step is `revise`. Run it.
- `review: needs_rework` → next_step is `execute`. Run it.
- `review: success` → state flips to `done`. Exit.
- Internal caps (3 revise cycles, 3 execute no-progress, 3 review rework) are enforced BY megaplan — the driver just follows `next_step`.

## Three places judgment could sneak in — all have a clean default

1. **`gate: ESCALATE`**. Megaplan asks: force-proceed / add-note / abort. You already told me "just run it." Driver policy: **always force-proceed on escalate**. That's your documented preference.

2. **A phase literally fails** (codex API error, transient network). Default next_step doesn't change. Driver would loop forever running the same failed phase. Fix: **detect "same state 5 iterations in a row without progress → bail and alert"**. Not judgment — mechanical.

3. **`execute` is per-batch**. If megaplan produces N batches, running `megaplan execute` without `--batch` runs all of them sequentially. Already handled internally. Confirmed earlier in our previous megaplan run.

## The one thing that's NOT a judgment but worth naming

Gate returning `PROCEED` with preflight FAIL — megaplan says "fix the blocking checks via revise." Driver just follows `next_step` (which will be `revise` in this case). Works mechanically.

## Verdict

**No real judgment.** Your "just run it" preference maps cleanly to: follow `next_step` always, force-proceed on escalate, bail after 5 stalls. That's option A with 8 extra lines of defensive logic.

  "content": "\"\"\"Auto-driver that advances a plan through its phases without human intervention.\n\nThis is the mechanical loop that most orchestrators end up writing by hand:\nread `status`, run `next_step`, repeat until terminal. All real judgment is\ndelegated to megaplan's existing phase logic — the driver only applies two\ndocumented defaults:\n\n1. Gate ESCALATE → force-proceed (caller opts out with ``--on-escalate abort``\n   or ``--on-escalate fail``).\n2. Same state for N consecutive iterations → bail (stall detection).\n\nThe driver is intentionally dumb. If a run needs judgment the driver can't\nprovide, it exits with a non-zero status and prints the state snapshot so the\ncaller can intervene.\n\"\"\"\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport argparse\nimport json\nimport subprocess\nimport sys\nimport time\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nfrom pathlib import Path\nfrom typing import Any\n\nfrom megaplan.types import TERMINAL_STATES\n\n\nDEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD = 5\nDEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS = 200\nDEFAULT_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS = 1.0\nESCALATE_ACTIONS = (\"force-proceed\", \"abort\", \"fail\")\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass DriverOutcome:\n    \"\"\"Terminal outcome reported when the loop exits.\"\"\"\n\n    status: str  # \"done\" | \"stalled\" | \"escalated\" | \"failed\" | \"aborted\" | \"cap\"\n    plan: str\n    final_state: str\n    iterations: int\n    reason: str = \"\"\n    last_phase: str | None = None\n    events: list[dict[str, Any]] = field(default_factory=list)\n\n    def to_json(self) -> str:\n        return json.dumps(\n            {\n                \"status\": self.status,\n                \"plan\": self.plan,\n                \"final_state\": self.final_state,\n                \"iterations\": self.iterations,\n                \"reason\": self.reason,\n                \"last_phase\": self.last_phase,\n                \"events\": self.events,\n            },\n            indent=2,\n        )\n\n\ndef _run_megaplan(args: list[str], *, cwd: Path | None = None) -> tuple[int, str, str]:\n    \"\"\"Run a megaplan sub-command in its own process.\n\n    We shell out rather than importing the handlers directly so each phase gets\n    a fresh argparse/handler lifecycle. This matches how external orchestrators\n    drive the CLI and avoids subtle state leakage between phases.\n    \"\"\"\n    proc = subprocess.run(\n        [\"megaplan\", *args],\n        cwd=str(cwd) if cwd else None,\n        capture_output=True,\n        text=True,\n        check=False,\n    )\n    return proc.returncode, proc.stdout, proc.stderr\n\n\ndef _status(plan: str, cwd: Path | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]:\n    code, out, err = _run_megaplan([\"status\", \"--plan\", plan], cwd=cwd)\n    if code != 0:\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"megaplan status failed (exit {code}): {err.strip() or out.strip()}\")\n    return json.loads(out)\n\n\ndef _has_valid_next(status: dict[str, Any], action: str) -> bool:\n    return action in (status.get(\"valid_next\") or [])\n\n\ndef _phase_command(next_step: str) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"Translate a `next_step` from status into the CLI args that run it.\n\n    Most phases are one-to-one: next_step == command. Execute adds the\n    destructive + user-approved flags because auto-mode implies both.\n    \"\"\"\n    if next_step == \"execute\":\n        return [\"execute\", \"--confirm-destructive\", \"--user-approved\"]\n    return [next_step]\n\n\ndef drive(\n    plan: str,\n    *,\n    cwd: Path | None = None,\n    stall_threshold: int = DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD,\n    max_iterations: int = DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS,\n    on_escalate: str = \"force-proceed\",\n    poll_sleep: float = DEFAULT_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS,\n    writer=sys.stdout.write,\n) -> DriverOutcome:\n    \"\"\"Drive ``plan`` to completion.\n\n    Returns a DriverOutcome with a terminal status. The writer is used for\n    human-readable progress; structured events are collected on the outcome.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    if on_escalate not in ESCALATE_ACTIONS:\n        raise ValueError(f\"on_escalate must be one of {ESCALATE_ACTIONS}\")\n\n    events: list[dict[str, Any]] = []\n    last_state: str | None = None\n    stall_count = 0\n    last_phase: str | None = None\n\n    def log(msg: str, **fields: Any) -> None:\n        events.append({\"msg\": msg, **fields})\n        writer(f\"[auto {plan}] {msg}\\n\")\n\n    for iteration in range(1, max_iterations + 1):\n        try:\n            status = _status(plan, cwd=cwd)\n        except (RuntimeError, json.JSONDecodeError) as error:\n            log(f\"status lookup failed: {error}\")\n            return DriverOutcome(\n                status=\"failed\",\n                plan=plan,\n                final_state=last_state or \"unknown\",\n                iterations=iteration,\n                reason=str(error),\n                last_phase=last_phase,\n                events=events,\n            )\n\n        state = status.get(\"state\", \"\")\n        next_step = status.get(\"next_step\")\n        valid_next = status.get(\"valid_next\") or []\n\n        log(\n            f\"iter {iteration} state={state} next={next_step} valid_next={valid_next}\",\n            iteration=iteration,\n            state=state,\n            next_step=next_step,\n            valid_next=valid_next,\n        )\n\n        # Terminal: plan reached a final state.\n        if state in TERMINAL_STATES:\n            log(f\"terminal state reached: {state}\")\n            return DriverOutcome(\n                status=\"done\" if state == \"done\" else \"aborted\",\n                plan=plan,\n                final_state=state,\n                iterations=iteration,\n                reason=f\"plan entered terminal state '{state}'\",\n                last_phase=last_phase,\n                events=events,\n            )\n\n        # Stall detection: same state for stall_threshold+ iterations.\n        if state == last_state:\n            stall_count += 1\n            if stall_count >= stall_threshold:\n                log(f\"stalled at state={state} for {stall_count} iterations\")\n                return DriverOutcome(\n                    status=\"stalled\",\n                    plan=plan,\n                    final_state=state,\n                    iterations=iteration,\n                    reason=(\n                        f\"stalled at '{state}' for {stall_count} iterations — \"\n                        \"manual intervention required\"\n                    ),\n                    last_phase=last_phase,\n                    events=events,\n                )\n        else:\n            stall_count = 0\n            last_state = state\n\n        # Escalation: no phase to run but overrides are available.\n        if not next_step:\n            if _has_valid_next(status, \"override force-proceed\"):\n                if on_escalate == \"force-proceed\":\n                    log(\"gate escalated — force-proceeding (per on_escalate=force-proceed)\")\n                    code, out, err = _run_megaplan(\n                        [\n                            \"override\",\n                            \"force-proceed\",\n                            \"--plan\",\n                            plan,\n                            \"--reason\",\n                            \"megaplan auto: escalate → force-proceed\",\n                        ],\n                        cwd=cwd,\n                    )\n                    if code != 0:\n                        log(f\"force-proceed failed (exit {code}): {err.strip() or out.strip()}\")\n                        return DriverOutcome(\n                            status=\"failed\",\n                            plan=plan,\n                            final_state=state,\n                            iterations=iteration,\n                            reason=f\"override force-proceed exited {code}\",\n                            last_phase=last_phase,\n                            events=events,\n                        )\n                    continue\n                if on_escalate == \"abort\":\n                    log(\"gate escalated — aborting (per on_escalate=abort)\")\n                    _run_megaplan(\n                        [\n                            \"override\",\n                            \"abort\",\n                            \"--plan\",\n                            plan,\n                            \"--reason\",\n                            \"megaplan auto: escalate → abort\",\n                        ],\n                        cwd=cwd,\n                    )\n                    return DriverOutcome(\n                        status=\"aborted\",\n                        plan=plan,\n                        final_state=state,\n                        iterations=iteration,\n                        reason=\"gate escalated and on_escalate=abort\",\n                        last_phase=last_phase,\n                        events=events,\n                    )\n                # on_escalate == \"fail\"\n                log(\"gate escalated — failing (per on_escalate=fail)\")\n                return DriverOutcome(\n                    status=\"escalated\",\n                    plan=plan,\n                    final_state=state,\n                    iterations=iteration,\n                    reason=\"gate escalated and on_escalate=fail — human required\",\n                    last_phase=last_phase,\n                    events=events,\n                )\n            log(f\"no next_step and no override available (valid_next={valid_next})\")\n            return DriverOutcome(\n                status=\"failed\",\n                plan=plan,\n                final_state=state,\n                iterations=iteration,\n                reason=\"no next_step and no override available\",\n                last_phase=last_phase,\n                events=events,\n            )\n\n        # Run the next phase.\n        cmd = _phase_command(next_step) + [\"--plan\", plan]\n        log(f\"running: megaplan {' '.join(cmd)}\", phase=next_step)\n        last_phase = next_step\n        code, out, err = _run_megaplan(cmd, cwd=cwd)\n        if code != 0:\n            # Don't bail immediately — megaplan often records a partial failure\n            # in state.json and the next status() reveals a recoverable valid_next.\n            # Stall detection will still kill infinite loops.\n            log(f\"phase '{next_step}' exited {code}: {err.strip() or out.strip()[-400:]}\")\n        if poll_sleep > 0:\n            time.sleep(poll_sleep)\n\n    # Hit iteration cap.\n    log(f\"hit max_iterations={max_iterations}\")\n    return DriverOutcome(\n        status=\"cap\",\n        plan=plan,\n        final_state=last_state or \"unknown\",\n        iterations=max_iterations,\n        reason=f\"exceeded max_iterations={max_iterations}\",\n        last_phase=last_phase,\n        events=events,\n    )\n\n\ndef build_auto_parser(subparsers: Any) -> None:\n    auto_parser = subparsers.add_parser(\n        \"auto\",\n        help=\"Drive a plan to completion without human intervention\",\n    )\n    auto_parser.add_argument(\"--plan\", required=True, help=\"Plan name\")\n    auto_parser.add_argument(\n        \"--stall-threshold\",\n        type=int,\n        default=DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD,\n        help=f\"Exit if the plan state doesn't change for this many iterations (default {DEFAULT_STALL_THRESHOLD})\",\n    )\n    auto_parser.add_argument(\n        \"--max-iterations\",\n        type=int,\n        default=DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS,\n        help=f\"Hard cap on loop iterations (default {DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS})\",\n    )\n    auto_parser.add_argument(\n        \"--on-escalate\",\n        choices=ESCALATE_ACTIONS,\n        default=\"force-proceed\",\n        help=\"What to do when the gate escalates (default force-proceed)\",\n    )\n    auto_parser.add_argument(\n        \"--poll-sleep\",\n        type=float,\n        default=DEFAULT_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS,\n        help=f\"Seconds to sleep between phase transitions (default {DEFAULT_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS})\",\n    )\n\n\ndef run_auto(root: Path, args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:\n    \"\"\"CLI entry point. Returns a POSIX exit code suitable for ``sys.exit``.\"\"\"\n    outcome = drive(\n        args.plan,\n        cwd=root,\n        stall_threshold=args.stall_threshold,\n        max_iterations=args.max_iterations,\n        on_escalate=args.on_escalate,\n        poll_sleep=args.poll_sleep,\n    )\n    sys.stdout.write(outcome.to_json() + \"\\n\")\n    if outcome.status == \"done\":\n        return 0\n    if outcome.status == \"aborted\":\n        return 0  # user-requested abort is not a failure\n    if outcome.status == \"stalled\":\n        return 2\n    if outcome.status == \"escalated\":\n        return 3\n    if outcome.status == \"cap\":\n        return 4\n    return 1\n"
}
